blocks.text: A baby boy was well for his first six months. Then came an ear infection, then pneumonia, then another pneumonia, each caused by a bacterium with a polysaccharide capsule, each needing hospital treatment. His older brother had died in infancy of a similar illness. Which arm of immunity is failing, and what single blood test would you ask for first?

blocks.markdown: **Primary immunodeficiencies** are inherited defects of immune function. More than four hundred are described, and most are rare. Clinically, the **pattern of infection** points to the failing component, which is the key skill in this unit: ask *which organisms, which sites, when it began and how severe*. Immunodeficiency should be considered when infections are unusually frequent, severe, persistent, unusual in organism, or respond poorly to treatment.

rows: Recurrent sinopulmonary infections with encapsulated bacteria (Streptococcus pneumoniae, Haemophilus influenzae); enteroviruses; Giardia
After about 6 months, when maternal IgG wanes
X-linked agammaglobulinaemia, common variable immunodeficiency, selective IgA deficiency
Viral (CMV, EBV, adenovirus), fungal (Candida, Pneumocystis), mycobacterial, protozoal; failure to thrive, chronic diarrhoea
Skin and organ abscesses, recurrent bacterial and fungal infection (Staphylococcus aureus, Aspergillus), poor wound healing, delayed umbilical cord separation
Chronic granulomatous disease, leucocyte adhesion deficiency
Neisseria infections (terminal); pyogenic infection (C3); immune complex disease (early components)
blocks.caption: Matching a pattern of infection to the arm of immunity

blocks.title: Which arm is failing?
blocks.prompt: A 2-year-old boy has had five episodes of otitis media and two of sinusitis, with Haemophilus influenzae cultured, plus a prolonged episode of giardiasis. He is growing normally, has no thrush, and has had no unusual viral infections. Which arm is most likely affected and which test do you request?

steps.text: Identify the organism type: recurrent infections with encapsulated bacteria such as Haemophilus at sinopulmonary sites point to a failure of opsonising antibody (B cell arm).
Note the pattern: respiratory-tract infections with encapsulated bacteria plus Giardia, appearing after infancy (when maternal IgG has declined), are typical of antibody deficiency.
Exclude T cell failure: thriving, no thrush and no opportunistic infections argue against a major T cell defect.
Order tests: quantitative serum immunoglobulins (IgG, IgA, IgM) and B cell counts (CD19⁺ cells by flow cytometry). Absent B cells with very low immunoglobulins suggests X-linked agammaglobulinaemia.

blocks.answer: Antibody (B cell) deficiency; test serum immunoglobulins and B cell numbers.

blocks.markdown: **X-linked agammaglobulinaemia (XLA, Bruton).** Caused by mutations in the **BTK gene** (Bruton tyrosine kinase) on the X chromosome. BTK is needed for pre-B cell receptor signalling, so B cell development stops at the **pre-B cell** stage in the bone marrow. There are almost no mature B cells (CD19⁺ cells <1%) and all immunoglobulin classes are very low. Boys present after about 6 months with recurrent bacterial sinopulmonary infections; tonsils and lymph nodes are small because there are no germinal centres. T cell function is normal. Treatment is lifelong **immunoglobulin replacement** (intravenous or subcutaneous) and prompt antibiotic treatment. Affected boys are inherited from carrier mothers; each son of a carrier has a 50% chance of being affected.

**Severe combined immunodeficiency (SCID).** A group of disorders in which T cell development fails, with or without B and NK cell defects. Because T cells are needed for cell-mediated immunity and for B cell help, immunity of both arms fails. Causes include **IL2RG** mutation (common gamma chain; X-linked and the most common form), **adenosine deaminase (ADA)** deficiency, and **RAG1/RAG2** mutation. Infants present in the first months of life with **failure to thrive, persistent diarrhoea, oral candidiasis, severe viral infections and Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia**. There is **lymphopenia** and the thymic shadow may be absent on chest imaging. It is a **paediatric emergency**; without **haematopoietic stem cell transplantation** (or gene therapy or enzyme replacement in some forms) it is fatal in infancy. Newborn screening in some countries measures T cell receptor excision circles (TRECs).

All types: bacterial, viral, fungal, opportunistic
B cells absent; T cells normal
T cells low or absent: lymphopenia

Absolute lymphocyte count (ALC) from total white cell count and lymphocyte fraction

blocks.title: Reading a blood count in a sick infant
blocks.prompt: A 2-month-old girl has failure to thrive, oral thrush and persistent diarrhoea. Her white cell count is 9.0 × 10^9/L with 8% lymphocytes. Calculate the absolute lymphocyte count and interpret it. (Healthy infants of this age normally have markedly higher lymphocyte counts than adults; ranges vary by laboratory but are roughly above 3 × 10^9/L.)

steps.text: Convert the percentage to a fraction.
Multiply by the white cell count.
Compare with the expected infant range: 0.72 × 10^9/L is far below it, so there is marked lymphopenia.

Interpretation: infant with failure to thrive, thrush and diarrhoea and severe lymphopenia is SCID until proved otherwise; urgent immunological referral, avoidance of live vaccines and irradiated blood products are needed.

blocks.answer: ALC 0.72 × 10^9/L: severe lymphopenia, so suspect SCID.

blocks.markdown: **Live vaccines and T cell deficiency.** Live attenuated vaccines (BCG, MMR, varicella, oral polio, rotavirus, oral typhoid) contain weakened organisms that replicate in the host. In a healthy person T cell and antibody responses control and eventually clear them. In **severe T cell deficiency** the organism cannot be cleared, so it can **replicate unchecked and cause disseminated, potentially fatal disease**, such as disseminated BCG infection or vaccine-strain rotavirus diarrhoea. Live vaccines are therefore **contraindicated** until severe T cell deficiency has been excluded in a child with suspected immunodeficiency, and in recipients with known SCID. Inactivated and subunit vaccines cannot replicate and are safe, although the response may be weaker.

blocks.title: Do not delay the suspicion
blocks.text: If a baby has features of SCID, the live vaccines due at birth or in the first months (such as BCG or rotavirus in some schedules) should be withheld until immunological assessment, since vaccine-strain infection can be fatal.

points: The pattern of infection indicates the failing arm: antibody deficiency gives recurrent encapsulated bacterial infections after 6 months; T cell deficiency gives early severe viral, fungal and opportunistic infections; phagocyte defects give abscesses; complement defects give Neisseria.

XLA is a BTK defect with absent B cells and very low immunoglobulins; SCID is a failure of T cell development (e.g. IL2RG, ADA, RAG) presenting in early infancy and fatal without stem cell transplantation.
Live vaccines are contraindicated in severe T cell deficiency because the vaccine organism cannot be cleared and may disseminate.

questions.stem: A 3-year-old has recurrent deep skin abscesses and invasive aspergillosis. Which arm of immunity is most likely defective?

distractorRationale.a: Antibody defects cause encapsulated bacterial sinopulmonary infection.
distractorRationale.b: T cell defects cause viral, fungal and opportunistic infections but typically with failure to thrive and not abscesses.
distractorRationale.c: Correct: abscesses with S. aureus and fungi suggest a phagocyte killing defect.
distractorRationale.d: Terminal complement defects cause Neisserial infection.

questions.explanation: Deep abscesses and invasive fungal infection with catalase-positive organisms point to a phagocyte killing defect such as chronic granulomatous disease.

questions.stem: A boy has had three bacterial pneumonias since the age of 8 months. Immunoglobulin levels are low, and CD19⁺ B cells are absent. Which diagnosis is most likely?

distractorRationale.a: SCID presents earlier with T cell failure and opportunistic infection.
distractorRationale.b: Correct: absent B cells, low immunoglobulins and onset after maternal IgG wanes fit XLA.
distractorRationale.c: C5 deficiency causes Neisserial infections and normal B cells.
distractorRationale.d: CGD causes abscesses and fungal infections, not low immunoglobulins.

questions.explanation: XLA results from BTK mutation, blocking B cell maturation. Boys present after about 6 months with recurrent bacterial infections, and B cells and immunoglobulins are absent or very low.

questions.stem: Which finding best supports SCID in a 3-month-old infant?

options.text: Normal growth and a normal lymphocyte count
Failure to thrive, persistent oral candidiasis and severe lymphopenia
A single episode of otitis media

questions.correctOptionText: Failure to thrive, persistent oral candidiasis and severe lymphopenia

distractorRationale.b: Correct: features of T cell failure with lymphopenia.
distractorRationale.c: Isolated IgA deficiency is common and often asymptomatic.
distractorRationale.d: One ear infection is normal in infancy.

questions.explanation: SCID presents in early infancy with failure to thrive, opportunistic infections such as candidiasis and Pneumocystis, persistent diarrhoea and lymphopenia.

questions.stem: What is the underlying defect in X-linked agammaglobulinaemia?

options.text: Mutation of BTK blocking B cell maturation at the pre-B cell stage

questions.correctOptionText: Mutation of BTK blocking B cell maturation at the pre-B cell stage

distractorRationale.a: Correct: BTK is required for pre-B cell receptor signalling.
distractorRationale.c: NADPH oxidase failure causes chronic granulomatous disease.

questions.explanation: BTK is needed for signalling by the pre-B cell receptor. Without it B cells fail to mature, so there is little antibody.

questions.stem: Why is a live attenuated vaccine dangerous in a baby with SCID?

options.text: The vaccine organism cannot be cleared by T cells and may replicate and disseminate
The vaccine is inactivated by maternal IgG
Live vaccines cause IgE-mediated anaphylaxis in all such patients
The baby will mount an excessive immune response

questions.correctOptionText: The vaccine organism cannot be cleared by T cells and may replicate and disseminate

distractorRationale.a: Correct: lack of T cell control allows replication and dissemination.
distractorRationale.b: Maternal IgG does not explain the danger.
distractorRationale.d: The problem is deficient, not excessive, response.

questions.explanation: Live vaccines contain replicating organisms. T cells normally control them; with SCID there is no such control, so disseminated vaccine-strain infection can be fatal.

questions.stem: True or false: inactivated vaccines are contraindicated in all patients with SCID because they can replicate.
questions.explanation: Inactivated and subunit vaccines cannot replicate and are not contraindicated for that reason, although responses may be poor. It is live attenuated vaccines that are contraindicated in severe T cell deficiency.

questions.stem: A 3-month-old infant with suspected immunodeficiency has a white cell count of 7.5 × 10^9/L with 10% lymphocytes. Calculate the absolute lymphocyte count in × 10^9/L.
questions.explanation: ALC = 7.5 × 0.10 = 0.75 × 10^9/L. This is much lower than the typical infant range (laboratory ranges vary), indicating lymphopenia that should prompt immunological assessment.

questions.stem: A woman is a carrier of X-linked agammaglobulinaemia and her partner is unaffected. What is the probability, in percent, that a given son is affected?
questions.explanation: The carrier mother passes the mutant X to a son with probability 1/2, and sons receive their X only from the mother, so each son has a 50% chance of being affected. Daughters are usually carriers or unaffected.

questions.stem: Match each of the following patterns of recurrent infection to the arm of immunity most likely to be affected and give a likely example of a defect: (a) pneumococcal pneumonia from 8 months, (b) severe Pneumocystis pneumonia at 2 months, (c) recurrent Neisseria meningitidis meningitis in a teenager.
markingGuide: Links organism/site/age to arm of immunity
questions.explanation: The pattern of organism, site and age of onset identifies the arm of immunity affected.

questions.stem: Compare X-linked agammaglobulinaemia and severe combined immunodeficiency in genetic cause, timing, infection pattern and treatment.
markingGuide: XLA: BTK defect, X-linked, B cells absent, onset after 6 months, bacterial sinopulmonary, immunoglobulin replacement
SCID: T cell development failure (IL2RG, ADA, RAG), early months, broad opportunistic infections and failure to thrive, lymphopenia, stem cell transplantation
Explains difference by arm of immunity
questions.explanation: XLA affects antibody only and is manageable with replacement; SCID affects both arms and needs transplantation.
